title: Resources
text:
All labs use STATA on your own laptop. The course do-files use official Stata commands (regress, teffects, sem, xtreg, ivregress, margins, permute). If your Stata is older than the version declared at the top of a do-file (version ...), change that line to your own version.


Only one user-written command is used in the labs (fre, Session 2, which tab1 can replace); the others are optional conveniences mentioned in the do-files:
* Session 2 — frequency tables with labels (or use tab1)
ssc install fre, replace

* Sessions 3 and 4 — coefficient plots
ssc install coefplot, replace

* Session 4 — fast regressions with many fixed effects
ssc install ftools, replace
ssc install reghdfe, replace
If ssc install fails on the university network, try again from a different connection or download the package files from SSC and install them with net install.



Assignments and the final paper must be accompanied by a do-file that reproduces all results. A minimal structure:
* ------------------------------------------------------------
* Project:  <title>
* Author:   <name>
* Date:     <date>
* Purpose:  reproduces all tables and figures in the paper
* ------------------------------------------------------------
version 18
clear all
set more off
set seed 20262027

* Paths: change only this line
global root "C:/Users/<you>/qmm2627_assignment1"

use "$root/data/mydata.dta", clear

* 1. Data preparation
* 2. Descriptives
* 3. Main models
* 4. Robustness and diagnostics
Set version to the Stata version you use, always set a seed when results depend on randomization (bootstrap, randomization inference, matching with ties), and never hard-code paths inside the analysis.

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Programme
PhD in Politics — second year


Period
First semester, 2026-2027


Instructor
Francesco Visconti


Field
Methods of Political Research


Software
STATA (on your own laptop)

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Applying knowledge and understanding
Students will be able to understand advanced quantitative methods relevant to their doctoral dissertations or research projects, and to specify, estimate, diagnose and interpret in STATA a measurement model, a difference-in-differences design, a regression discontinuity design and an instrumental variables estimation, reporting the results according to disciplinary standards.

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Making judgements
Through the discussion of published applications and replications, students will learn to assess the credibility of others’ identifying assumptions and to choose knowingly the analytical strategy best suited to their own research question, recognising when the available data do not support a causal answer.

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Communication skills
Students will improve their ability to present and discuss the results of their quantitative analyses, refining oral and written communication skills with particular attention to clarity and accuracy in data presentation.

title: Luiss Guido Carli | PhD in Politics | Quantitative Methods Masterclass
text:
Learning skills
The course fosters autonomy in methodological updating, training students to read recent methodological literature, to consult software documentation and to work with replicable code.

title: Sessions
text:
Readings marked as Optional are for further study and are not required for class discussion. The Applications are the studies discussed in class and used in the labs. Slides, do-files and data are added to each session as the course progresses.


Session 1 — Beyond control variables
Regression, identification and selection on observables

The course in one question: where does a credible comparison come from, and what must we believe for it to hold? What a regression coefficient actually estimates: potential outcomes, selection bias and identification as finding the right variation. Selection on observables and conditional independence. Causal diagrams as a tool for choosing controls: forks, chains and colliders, back doors and front doors; good and bad controls (mediators, colliders, and samples selected on them). The Table 2 fallacy: in a model built to identify one effect, the coefficients of the controls are not effects. Regression, matching and weighting as different estimators of the same assumption. When selection on observables is not credible: more similar units, falsification tests, sensitivity analysis, or a different source of variation (Sessions 3–5).

STATA lab: simulated data from a known causal diagram (university degree, cosmopolitan identity and EU support): four regressions (naive, with the confounder, with the mediator, on a sample selected on a collider) compared with the true effect; the Table 2 fallacy; the same assumption with different estimators, teffects ra and teffects ipw; balance with tebalance summarize.


Materials


Slides Session 1

Do-file



Readings

Keele, L., Stevenson, R. T., & Elwert, F. (2020). The Causal Interpretation of Estimated Associations in Regression Models. Political Science Research and Methods, 8(1), 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1017/psrm.2019.31
Huntington-Klein, N. (2022). The Effect: An Introduction to Research Design and Causality. CRC Press, chs. 5, 8 and 13. Open access: https://theeffectbook.net



Optional readings

Cinelli, C., & Hazlett, C. (2020). Making Sense of Sensitivity: Extending Omitted Variable Bias. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, 82(1), 39–67. https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12348
Montgomery, J. M., Nyhan, B., & Torres, M. (2018). How Conditioning on Posttreatment Variables Can Ruin Your Experiment and What to Do About It. American Journal of Political Science, 62(3), 760–775. https://doi.org/10.1111/ajps.12357




Session 2 — Measuring concepts
From indices to confirmatory factor analysis, and measurement invariance

What it means to measure a concept well: from the background concept to the indicators and the scores, systematic and random error, and three ways to gather evidence of validity (Adcock & Collier 2001); the same indicator in different contexts. Why an index with a good alpha is not enough: reliability is not unidimensionality. Principal component factoring, mean indices and factor scores. The confirmatory model: the common factor model, EFA and CFA side by side, specification and estimation in Stata, the standardized solution, fit indices, modification indices and the risk of capitalising on chance; how to present and report a CFA. Comparing groups: configural, metric and scalar invariance in a multiple-group CFA (optional material, not covered in class).

STATA lab (Acock 2013, ch. 1): ten items on the role of government (NLSY97). alpha and factor, pcf before CFA; a one-factor CFA with sem, estat gof and estat mindices; a two-factor alternative. Optional, for home: a multiple-group CFA by gender with group() and estat ginvariant (Acock 2013, sec. 5.3).


Materials


Material Session 2


Readings

Acock, A. C. (2013). Discovering Structural Equation Modeling Using Stata. Stata Press, chs. 1 and 5.3.



Optional readings

Adcock, R., & Collier, D. (2001). Measurement Validity: A Shared Standard for Qualitative and Quantitative Research. American Political Science Review, 95(3), 529–546. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055401003100
Davidov, E., Meuleman, B., Cieciuch, J., Schmidt, P., & Billiet, J. (2014). Measurement Equivalence in Cross-National Research. Annual Review of Sociology, 40, 55–75. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-soc-071913-043137




Session 3 — The experimental benchmark
Experiments, survey experiments and conjoint designs

Randomization as the solution to the identification problem: why a lottery makes the selection term zero by design. What makes a design an experiment: Dunning’s three hallmarks, and the difference between true, natural and quasi-experiments. Where experiments happen, from control to realism: laboratory (Nugent 2020), lab-in-the-field (Grossman & Baldassarri 2012), survey and field experiments. Survey-experimental designs: anchoring vignettes (King et al. 2004), vignette experiments, list experiments, conjoint designs with AMCEs and marginal means (an energy-transition conjoint). Field experiments: what changes in a regression when the researcher assigns the treatment, balance checks and the role of covariates (Gerber, Green & Larimer 2008). Natural experiments with a true lottery (the Vietnam draft) and with as-if random assignment (Snow’s cholera study). Integrating qualitative methods and experiments: before, during and after the experiment; what the qualitative strand checks (treatment received, causal pathways, SUTVA, realism, causal-process observations); Paluck’s field experiment in eastern Congo.

STATA lab: anchoring vignettes on political efficacy in China and Mexico (ttest, tabstat); a list experiment in Afghanistan; AMCEs and marginal means from an immigration conjoint, with standard errors clustered by respondent (regress, margins); a field experiment on social pressure and turnout: the effect as a difference in means, balance checks, covariates and randomization inference with permute. For home: heterogeneity with interactions, margins and marginsplot.


Materials


Material Session 3


–>  –>  –>


Required readings

Mutz, D. C. (2011). Population-Based Survey Experiments. Princeton University Press, ch. 1.
Dunning, T. (2012). Natural experiments in the social sciences a design-based approach. Cambridge University Press, ch. 1.
Levy Paluck, E. (2010). The promising integration of qualitative methods and field experiments. The ANNALS of the American Academy of Political and Social Science, 628(1), 59-71. https://doi.org/10.1177/0002716209351510



Applications

Nugent, E. R. (2020). The Psychology of Repression and Polarization. World Politics, 72(2), 291–334.
Grossman, G., & Baldassarri, D. (2012). The Impact of Elections on Cooperation: Evidence from a Lab-in-the-Field Experiment in Uganda. American Journal of Political Science, 56(4), 964–985.
King, G., Murray, C. J. L., Salomon, J. A., & Tandon, A. (2004). Enhancing the Validity and Cross-Cultural Comparability of Measurement in Survey Research. American Political Science Review, 98(1), 191–207.
Blair, G., Imai, K., & Lyall, J. (2014). Comparing and Combining List and Endorsement Experiments: Evidence from Afghanistan. American Journal of Political Science, 58(4), 1043–1063.
Natili, M., Pellegata, A., & Visconti, F. (2026). What Kind of Energy Transition? Public Opinion Trade-offs between Economic Growth, Ecological Sustainability, and Equity. European Journal of Political Research. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1475676526100784
Gerber, A. S., Green, D. P., & Larimer, C. W. (2008). Social Pressure and Voter Turnout: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment. American Political Science Review, 102(1), 33–48.
Angrist, J. D. (1990). Lifetime Earnings and the Vietnam Era Draft Lottery. American Economic Review, 80(3), 313–336.
Paluck, E. L. (2010). Is It Better Not to Talk? Group Polarization, Extended Contact, and Perspective Taking in Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 36(9), 1170–1185.










Session 4 — From fixed effects to difference-in-differences
Fixed effects, DiD and parallel trends

Fixed effects as a research design: comparing units with themselves, so that whatever does not change cancels out, observed or not; two-way fixed effects. Difference-in-differences as an attempt to reconstruct the counterfactual that an experiment guarantees by design: Snow’s cholera data as the first DiD; the 2×2 table; three comparisons resting on three different assumptions (Card & Krueger 1994). The parallel trends assumption: what it implies, why it cannot be tested directly, and how prior trends, placebo tests and knowledge of the case make it credible. DiD as a regression with an interaction of two dummies. What can go wrong: compound treatments, anticipation, composition, spillovers, few treated units; staggered adoption only as a pointer. A published application: the boycott of The Sun in Merseyside after Hillsborough and Euroscepticism (Foos & Bischof 2022).

STATA lab: the minimum wage in New Jersey and Pennsylvania (Card & Krueger 1994): did the treatment happen; three comparisons and their assumptions; the same DiD estimate three ways (difference in changes, interaction in long data, two-way fixed effects with xtreg, fe); a control group the law did not touch as a placebo.


Materials


Material Session 4


Required readings

Huntington-Klein, N. (2022). The Effect. CRC Press, ch. 18. Open access: https://theeffectbook.net



Optional readings

Roth, J., Sant’Anna, P. H. C., Bilinski, A., & Poe, J. (2023). What’s Trending in Difference-in-Differences? A Synthesis of the Recent Econometrics Literature. Journal of Econometrics, 235(2), 2218–2244, sections 1–2. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jeconom.2023.03.008



Applications

Card, D., & Krueger, A. B. (1994). Minimum Wages and Employment: A Case Study of the Fast-Food Industry in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. American Economic Review, 84(4), 772–793.
Foos, F., & Bischof, D. (2022). Tabloid Media Campaigns and Public Opinion: Quasi-Experimental Evidence on Euroscepticism in England. American Political Science Review, 116(1), 19–37.







Session 5 — Regression discontinuity and instrumental variables
Finding a lottery at the cutoff, borrowing a randomizer

Two designs that use only the part of the treatment assigned by something outside the units’ choices. Regression discontinuity: a rule with a cutoff, and the comparison of units just above and just below it; continuity (nothing else changes at the cutoff) as the identifying assumption; the estimate as two regressions and one difference, with its uncertainty; placebo outcomes; strong internal validity, limited external validity. Instrumental variables: a back door that cannot be closed (schooling, ability and earnings); an instrument that moves the treatment and reaches the outcome only through it; first stage, reduced form and their ratio; two-stage least squares. The assumptions (relevance, independence, exclusion, monotonicity, SUTVA) and their epistemic status: only relevance can be checked in the data. What an instrument estimates: the effect for compliers (LATE), with a return to the draft lottery of Session 3. Weak instruments. Who invented instrumental variables. Two applications from political science: radical right success and mainstream party positions (Abou-Chadi & Krause 2020) and elite messages and support for European integration (Gabel & Scheve 2007). DiD, RDD and IV compared, and the role of knowledge of the case in all three.

STATA lab: RDD — do British MPs get rich in office? (Eggers & Hainmueller 2009): the picture first; the jump as the difference between two regressions; its confidence interval; a placebo outcome; Labour as an exercise. IV — a college nearby and the return to schooling (Card 1995): the OLS benchmark; the Wald estimate from four means; first stage and reduced form; ivregress 2sls and estat firststage.


Materials


Material Session 5


Required readings

Imai, K., & Bougher, L. D. (2021). Quantitative Social Science: An Introduction in Stata. Princeton University Press, sections 4.3.4 and 6.3.5 (regression discontinuity).
Cunningham, S. (2021). Causal Inference: The Mixtape. Yale University Press, ch. 7 (instrumental variables). Open access: https://mixtape.scunning.com



Optional readings

Huntington-Klein, N. (2022). The Effect: An Introduction to Research Design and Causality. CRC Press, chs. 19 and 20. Open access: https://theeffectbook.net



Applications

Eggers, A. C., & Hainmueller, J. (2009). MPs for Sale? Returns to Office in Postwar British Politics. American Political Science Review, 103(4), 513–533.
Card, D. (1995). Using Geographic Variation in College Proximity to Estimate the Return to Schooling. In L. N. Christofides, E. K. Grant & R. Swidinsky (eds.), Aspects of Labour Market Behaviour. University of Toronto Press.
Abou-Chadi, T., & Krause, W. (2020). The Causal Effect of Radical Right Success on Mainstream Parties’ Policy Positions: A Regression Discontinuity Approach. British Journal of Political Science, 50(3), 829–847. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0007123418000029
Gabel, M., & Scheve, K. (2007). Estimating the Effect of Elite Communications on Public Opinion Using Instrumental Variables. American Journal of Political Science, 51(4), 1013–1028. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5907.2007.00294.x




Session 6 — From numbers to cases
Multi-method research, mechanisms and transparency

What a well-identified estimate still cannot tell us: the mechanism, the measurement, the assumptions and the scope. Integration, not triangulation: one method gives the answer, the other does a specific job for it. Six ways of combining methods: qualitative work first; nested analysis, with cases chosen from a regression (Lieberman 2005; Mattingly 2016); cases for measurement; cases for mechanisms and the tests of process tracing; cases for identifying assumptions, a recap of Sessions 3–5; numbers inside a case study. Common ways to get it wrong. Case selection after a regression: typical, diverse, extreme, deviant, influential, most similar and most different cases, and what each is good for (Seawright & Gerring 2008). Transparency in the quantitative and the qualitative strand, and in their combination. The course in one slide.
The session includes a workshop in which students present the design of their final paper.

STATA lab: a regression as a map of the cases. Life expectancy and income in 63 countries (sysuse lifeexp): fitted values, residuals, Cook’s distance and dfbeta; typical, deviant, influential and extreme cases; back to the large-N model with a variable suggested by a deviant case. Then the British candidates of Session 5: which biographies would you study, and why?


Materials
Slides, do-file and data will be posted here.



Required readings

Lieberman, E. S. (2005). Nested Analysis as a Mixed-Method Strategy for Comparative Research. American Political Science Review, 99(3), 435–452. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055405051762
Seawright, J., & Gerring, J. (2008). Case Selection Techniques in Case Study Research: A Menu of Qualitative and Quantitative Options. Political Research Quarterly, 61(2), 294–308. https://doi.org/10.1177/1065912907313077
Seawright, J. (2016). Multi-Method Social Science: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Tools. Cambridge University Press, chs. 1 and 4.



Optional readings

Goertz, G. (2017). Multimethod Research, Causal Mechanisms, and Case Studies. Princeton University Press, chs. 1–2.
Weller, N., & Barnes, J. (2014). Finding Pathways: Mixed-Method Research for Studying Causal Mechanisms. Cambridge University Press, ch. 1.



Applications

Mattingly, D. C. (2016). Elite Capture: How Decentralization and Informal Institutions Weaken Property Rights in China. World Politics, 68(3), 383–412.
Kreuzer, M. (2010). Historical Knowledge and Quantitative Analysis: The Case of the Origins of Proportional Representation. American Political Science Review, 104(2), 369–392.
Eggers, A. C., & Hainmueller, J. (2009). MPs for Sale? Returns to Office in Postwar British Politics. American Political Science Review, 103(4), 513–533.

title: Assessment
text:
Attendance and active participation are required. In case of justified absence, please inform the instructor in advance.
The final grade is expressed in thirtieths (/30). The pass mark is 18/30 and the maximum grade is 30/30 cum laude.








Component
Weight
Covers




Participation
10%
All sessions


Assignment 1 — Measure and control
20%
Sessions 1–2


Assignment 2 — Design or assess?
20%
Sessions 3–5


Final paper
50%
One method of the course applied to your own research




Participation (10%)
Attendance and active engagement in class discussions. Come to class having read the required readings for the session.


Assignments (40%, 20% each)
Two short papers, each built around your own doctoral project: a causal relationship, a concept or a causal claim that your thesis analyses, assumes or builds on. Each assignment offers a choice of tracks; most tracks are theoretical and need no data or software.

Measure and control (Sessions 1–2), 1,000 words max. Three tracks: Control, a causal diagram for a causal question from your thesis and the controls it implies; Measure on paper, a measurement design for a concept from your research; Measure with data, a confirmatory factor analysis in Stata on real survey data, following the Session 2 lab (with a do-file and the dataset).
Design or assess? (Sessions 3–5), 800 words max. Two tracks: Design, a study on paper that could answer a causal question from your thesis with one of the designs of Sessions 3–5 (an experiment, a natural experiment, difference-in-differences, an instrumental variable or a regression discontinuity); Assess, a judgement of how far the design of one published study supports its causal claim. Replicating the published analysis is optional.

Assignments are assessed on the correct use of the tools, the quality of the justification of each choice, transparency and clarity.



Final paper (50%)
A methodological paper of up to 3,000 words in which students apply one of the course methods to their own doctoral research question. The paper must:

motivate the choice of design;
state the identifying assumptions;
discuss their plausibility in the student’s case.

Reproducibility is also assessed: the paper must be accompanied by code and data, or by instructions for obtaining them. Students present the design of their final paper in the workshop held during Session 6: three minutes each, no slides, covering the question, the method and the data, the identifying assumption, the evidence for it, and what a case study would add.
